Paragraph:
Translation: If, however, you think that the soul is perpetually born and always dies, still you have no reason to lament, O mighty-armed.

Purport (Excerpt): There is always a class of philosophers, almost akin to the Buddhists, who do not believe in the separate existence of the soul beyond the body... According to them, the body is a combination of physical elements, and at a certain stage the life symptoms develop by interaction of the physical and chemical elements... Even if Arjuna did not believe in the existence of the soul... there would still have been no cause for lamentation. No one laments the loss of a certain bulk of chemicals.
Situation/Problem_Faced: Krishna anticipates that Arjuna might still doubt the Vedic concept of an eternal soul and might lean towards a purely materialistic worldview.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: Krishna adopts a devil's advocate approach (Lokayatikas/Vaibhasikas philosophy). He argues that even if life is just a random collision of chemicals that ends at death, grief is still illogical. One doesn't cry over the dispersal of chemicals.
Outcome/Resolution: Krishna blocks the escape route of atheistic doubt. He proves that whether one is a spiritualist or a materialist, lamentation in the face of duty is irrational.

Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.cognitive Flexibility: Approaching a problem from multiple belief systems
Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.logical Refutation: Breaking down the irrationality of an emotion
Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.stoicism: Accepting the material reality without emotional breakdown

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Lokayata / Vaibhasika (Materialistic philosophies denying the eternal soul)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: Krishna briefly entertains the materialistic theory that life is merely a byproduct of chemical interactions. He points out that even under this philosophy, death is just the dissolution of matter, which warrants no moral panic or grief, thus making Arjuna's paralyzing sorrow logically unfounded from any angle.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: This is a profound exercise in cognitive flexibility. When a person is trapped in anxiety, they often cycle through different 'what ifs'. Krishna takes Arjuna's worst-case 'what if' (what if there is no soul and this is all there is?) and shows that even in that scenario, his intense lamentation is illogical. It cuts off the anxiety loop at its root.
